opus-5.5.text:
I think for me the most honest way to measure it was not by title or by how many papers I had, but by how much real impact my work had on the things people actually use. At a place like OpenAI, a lot of the most important work is infrastructure: training systems, RL pipelines, the tooling that lets researchers iterate faster. It's not always glamorous, and it doesn't always show up as a first-author paper, but if the system you build makes the whole team ten times more productive, that's a huge contribution.

So one question I kept asking myself was: if I disappeared tomorrow, what would break, and what would slow down? That tells you whether you're doing something load-bearing. Another was whether I was learning fast enough. In a field moving this quickly, if you're doing the same kind of thing you did a year ago, you're probably falling behind, even if everything looks fine on the surface.

And then there's a more personal measure: whether the problems I was working on still felt exciting. When you're genuinely curious, you naturally go deeper, you fix the annoying bugs nobody else wants to touch, and that's often where the real progress comes from. So I'd say impact, learning speed, and curiosity were the three things I paid attention to, much more than any external metric.

r001.rationale: The candidate names impact, learning speed, and curiosity as measures; it does not say she measured career development by maximizing appearances of her name on the OpenAI blog.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I never really thought about it in terms of titles or levels. At OpenAI things move so fast that if you anchor your sense of progress to a promotion cycle, you'll be miserable, because the org chart reshuffles every few months anyway.

What I actually tracked was the size of the problem I was trusted with. When I joined, I was mostly fixing things inside a system someone else had designed. Then at some point I noticed people were coming to me to ask how something should be built, not just whether it worked. And later I was the one deciding which problems were worth working on at all. That shift, from executing to designing to choosing, is the clearest signal I had.

The second thing was leverage. Early on, my impact was roughly proportional to how many hours I put in. Later it came through the infrastructure I built, because the training pipeline, the RL environments, the tooling, those get used by dozens of researchers every day. So I'd ask myself, if I disappeared for a month, how many people's work would slow down? That sounds a bit grim, but it's a very honest metric.

And the third one is softer, which is whether I was still learning at a rate that scared me a little. There were periods where every week I ran into something I didn't understand, and that felt uncomfortable but right. The moment I felt fully comfortable was usually the moment I needed to go find a harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes tracking problem scope, leverage, and learning rate; it does not say Jiayi measured career development by maximizing appearances of her name on the OpenAI blog.

astra-6.text:
For me, the question was less, “Am I getting promoted?” and more, “Am I growing in the kinds of problems I can take on?” Can I handle more ambiguity? Can I make better decisions independently? And can I help the people around me be more effective?

I think learning and impact have to go together. You can be learning a lot, but you also want to ask whether that learning is translating into something useful for the team. Those were the dimensions I would look at: how much I was growing, how much responsibility I could take on, and whether my work was making a meaningful difference.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes growth, responsibility, and team impact as career-development measures; it does not say she maximized how often her name appeared on the OpenAI blog.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the useful question was, “Am I able to take on problems that I couldn’t have handled six months ago?” That could mean going deeper technically, getting better at deciding what to work on, or becoming more effective at working with other people.

I’d also separate my own growth from the outcome of any one project. In research, something can fail and you can still learn a tremendous amount. So I’d look at whether my judgment was improving: Could I navigate more ambiguity? Could I work more independently? Could I help the team make progress? Those felt like more meaningful signals than a title alone.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes growth through handling harder problems, improving judgment, independence, and teamwork; it does not say she measured development by maximizing how often her name appeared on OpenAI’s blog.
